effectiveness_notes: 78% reduction in crop raids when properly maintained. Effectiveness drops below 40% if maintenance intervals exceed 6 months.
maintenance_requirement: Monthly inspection; vegetation clearance every 6–8 weeks; annual battery replacement
limitations: Requires ongoing maintenance commitment
Initial capital cost may be prohibitive
Can be bypassed by elephants at damaged or unmaintained sections
implementation_notes: Solar-powered units outperform grid-connected units in remote areas with 23% better uptime. Community ownership models significantly improve fence longevity. DWC provides technical support for installation.

effectiveness_notes: 62% deterrence rate in dry conditions. Drops to 18% in heavy rainfall when bees do not emerge. Most effective as a secondary barrier combined with other methods.
cost_estimate: LKR 40,000–65,000 per km installed (excluding hive population cost)
suitable_for: areas where electric fencing is unaffordable
maintenance_requirement: Bi-weekly hive inspection; honey harvest every 3–4 months; hive replacement when colony collapses
limitations: Not effective in heavy rain or cool temperatures
Requires beekeeping knowledge
Bees can sting farmers
implementation_notes: Honey production generates approximately LKR 32,000 per km per year, offsetting installation costs. Community acceptance is high at 89% of pilot participants. Training in beekeeping is required before deployment.

effectiveness_notes: Effective as a short-term deterrent. Elephants habituate to chili barriers over time, reducing long-term effectiveness. Best used as a supplementary measure.
cost_estimate: LKR 8,000–15,000 per season (chili oil, rope, labour)
maintenance_requirement: Reapplication after rainfall; daily inspection during high-risk periods
limitations: Habituate elephants eventually learn to ignore it
Requires constant reapplication
Affected by rain and wind
implementation_notes: Chili barriers involve stringing ropes soaked in a mixture of chili and engine oil around field boundaries. Most effective when combined with noise deterrents and community watch systems. Used widely in Hambantota and Monaragala.

effectiveness_notes: Reduces human-elephant encounter injuries by 41% in pilot deployments. Average alert time reduced from 45 minutes to under 6 minutes when sensor-linked.
cost_estimate: LKR 120,000–200,000 per village system (sensors, server, community phones)
maintenance_requirement: Monthly sensor battery check; quarterly system calibration; community operator training annually
limitations: Requires mobile network coverage
Dependent on reliable power for sensors
Alert fatigue if too many false positives
implementation_notes: Systems combining infrared motion sensors with GSM transmitters send automated alerts to registered community members. Co-design with communities achieves 3× higher adoption than top-down implementation. Women farmers particularly benefit as they represent disproportionate risk during morning work hours.

effectiveness_notes: Effective when staffed consistently. Incidents at Lahugala reduced by community watch in 2023 — zero casualties despite herd raid due to advance warning.
cost_estimate: LKR 35,000–80,000 per tower (construction) + ongoing volunteer coordination
suitable_for: communities with strong social cohesion and volunteer capacity
maintenance_requirement: Nightly roster management; seasonal inspection of tower structure
limitations: Labour-intensive — requires nightly roster
Volunteer fatigue during extended raids
Visibility limited in dense vegetation
implementation_notes: Elevated watch platforms (5–8 metres) positioned at field edges allow scouts to detect elephants and alert the community. Most effective when integrated with noise deterrents (drums, firecrackers) and communication systems (radio, mobile phone). Used effectively at Lahugala (Ampara) and Kaudulla Buffer Zone (Polonnaruwa).

effectiveness_notes: Combined acoustic system (firecrackers + bee swarm playback) achieved 68% turn-back rate in early warning system pilots. Firecrackers alone: 45% turn-back rate.
maintenance_requirement: Replenish firecrackers seasonally; battery check for electronic units monthly
limitations: Elephants habituate to noise deterrents used repetitively
Noise disturbance to community and other wildlife
Firecrackers can be hazardous to users
implementation_notes: Rotating deterrent types (different sounds, locations) slows habituation. Electronic bee swarm recordings exploit elephants' documented fear of bees. Most effective when used as a response tool after SMS/watch alerts rather than as a constant deterrent.

method: Solar Lighting for Field Approaches and Village Perimeters
effectiveness_notes: Reduces risk to humans navigating fields at night. Does not directly deter elephants but significantly reduces the chance of surprise encounters.
suitable_for: areas with high night-time human movement
maintenance_requirement: Annual panel cleaning; battery replacement every 3–4 years
limitations: Does not prevent elephant entry
Only reduces human risk — not crop loss
implementation_notes: Solar motion-sensor lights along field approach paths alert farmers approaching fields at night. Primarily a human safety measure rather than an elephant deterrent. Most valuable in Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa where farmers access fields early morning and after dark.

effectiveness_notes: The highest-impact long-term mitigation measure identified in climate-change projections. Maintaining intact corridors reduces boundary violations by keeping elephants on established routes.
cost_estimate: Policy and land acquisition cost varies — LKR millions to billions depending on scope
maintenance_requirement: Ongoing enforcement of corridor designation; vegetation management; encroachment monitoring
limitations: Requires government-level policy action
Long time horizon for impact
Conflicts with agricultural and development land demand
implementation_notes: GPS telemetry research (Fernando et al., 2021) identified three primary movement corridors in the North-Central Province linking Wilpattu, Madhu, and Anuradhapura protected areas. Formalising and protecting these corridors is the recommended strategic priority over short-term deterrents.

method: Agricultural Crop Zoning Away from Corridor Boundaries
effectiveness_notes: Reduces frequency of encounters by creating buffer zones of less-attractive crops near park and corridor boundaries.
cost_estimate: Implementation depends on landholding patterns — low direct cost but income trade-off for farmers
maintenance_requirement: Annual review of crop patterns; farmer education and incentive programmes
limitations: Economically difficult for smallholders who need highest-yield areas
Requires community buy-in and compensation mechanisms
implementation_notes: Positioning non-preferred crops (capsicum, ginger, lemon grass, rubber) along forest-facing boundaries and high-value paddy fields towards the interior of cultivation areas reduces the attractiveness of boundary zones for raiding elephants. Most feasible when paired with crop diversification subsidies.

effectiveness_notes: Does not prevent conflict but reduces economic devastation. Current national uptake below 12% due to complex claims processes.
cost_estimate: Premium: LKR 3,000–8,000 per acre per season (government-subsidised schemes)
maintenance_requirement: Annual policy renewal; documentation of fields and crop values pre-season
limitations: Claims processes are bureaucratically complex
Current schemes cover only 23% of actual losses on average
Verification and fraud prevention mechanisms slow payouts
implementation_notes: Government compensation schemes and insurance products exist but are severely underutilised. Policy analysis (Jayasuriya & Cooray, 2024) recommends simplifying claims through mobile-based loss reporting and DWC field officer verification. Insurance combined with prevention investment yields better outcomes than either alone.

method: Safe Passage Guidelines and Community Education
effectiveness_notes: Reduces human fatalities by ensuring people know how to behave during elephant encounters. Does not prevent property or crop damage.
maintenance_requirement: Annual refresher sessions; updated materials as new findings emerge
limitations: Behaviour change is slow
High-stress situations override training for some individuals
implementation_notes: Key safety messages: do not attempt to chase elephants alone; avoid forest paths at dawn and dusk; never stand between an elephant and its calf; use a torch or mobile light when walking at night; call DWC hotline (DWC 24-hour line: 011-2888585). Women and children's exposure risk during early-morning field work is a key focus area identified in research (Dharmaratne et al., 2021).

method: AI-Powered HEC Incident Reporting and Pattern Analysis
effectiveness_notes: Centralised digital incident reporting enables pattern detection, hotspot mapping, and predictive risk assessment — currently absent from Sri Lanka's national HEC management system.
cost_estimate: LKR 3–8 million (system development); minimal marginal cost per report thereafter
maintenance_requirement: Regular model updates as new data is ingested; infrastructure maintenance
limitations: Requires consistent data input quality from field officers
Relies on mobile/internet connectivity in remote areas
Requires training and behaviour change among DWC staff
implementation_notes: A unified AI-powered knowledge system for HEC — combining natural language querying, historical incident analysis, and pattern detection — is identified as a critical infrastructure gap. Current data is siloed across DWC, media, and research sources with no central repository. The HEC Intelligence System being developed at the University of Moratuwa aims to address this gap.
